rationale: A wins because it finds the hardest, most reporter-shaped story in the fact set: 'The new enterprise question: which AI agents get write access?' That angle turns Airtable's record-updating agents into an enterprise IT risk story and names the proof that can kill it. B has useful bones, but 'The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market' turns one company's repositioning into a market verdict it cannot prove. A has a little swagger problem; B has a thesis-evidence problem.
gaps_in_A: 'bets the company on agents' overstates the supplied facts. A repositioning is not automatically an existential bet.
'established category leader' is not grounded in the update. 'Serves many enterprise teams' does not prove category leadership.
'only one whose proof you already hold' is too generous; the set itself says the repositioning angle still needs product-vs-messaging evidence and a spokesperson.
gaps_in_B: 'The no-code database market just became the AI-agent-on-your-data market' is the biggest overreach. One Airtable launch is a data point, not a market conversion.
'can an AI agent pivot close the gap from its peak?' invents motive. The update gives valuation context, not evidence that this launch is meant to repair the mark or create a liquidity path.

It misses the cleanest enterprise angle as an angle: write access, permissions, audit logs, rollback, and reliability. It only buries this in 'Is Airtable willing to share any reliability or error-rate data?'
The category and competitive angles blur together: 'where the no-code/low-code category is heading' and 'redraws the competitive map' are two envelopes around the same category-shift story.
